consensus_summary: The consensus identifies 'the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) as Jesus' tomb/grave — his death-and-burial interval before resurrection — often extended to Sheol/Hades as the realm of the dead, framed by the Jonah typology. A Jerusalem/'heart of the land' reading is explicitly listed by two responses as a minority or rare alternative tied to alternative passion chronologies.
book_summary: The book identifies 'the heart of the earth' as Jerusalem, the navel and heart of the land, citing Ezekiel 5:5 (Jerusalem set 'in the midst of the nations') and Ezekiel 38:12 ('dwell in the midst of the land'), and explicitly flags the grave/Hades reading as merely the common teaching it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: The grave/tomb (and by traditional extension Sheol/Hades) where Christ lay between death and resurrection.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem — the geographic/theological center ('navel/heart') of the land — as the place where the Son of Man spent three days and three nights.
boundary_disagreement: The disagreement is not about boundary conditions of a shared referent but about which referent the phrase names: a place of burial/the dead versus the city of Jerusalem. A Jerusalem reading typically relocates the three days and nights to include arrest, trials, and custody within the city, not merely (or not at all) the entombment.
material_contradiction: The book's own common-view note ('Commonly taught: the grave or Hades') marks its Jerusalem identification as a replacement of the consensus referent. 'Heart of the earth' cannot in the same sense denote both the tomb/underworld and the city of Jerusalem; accepting the book's core requires rejecting the consensus's core identification, even though both readings agree the saying concerns Christ's passion period.
rationale: Both cores concern Matt 12:40, but the book substitutes Jerusalem ('earth' as land) for the consensus's grave/Hades. This is precisely the minority reading Response A lists (with the same Ezekiel prooftexts) and Response B lists as rare, so it is a recognized but non-consensus position that contradicts, rather than refines, the settled core. Because the alternative is explicitly catalogued in the blind responses, the verdict is DIVERGENT rather than NOVEL.
strongest_objection: One could argue for REFINED on the grounds that the book keeps the same event-complex (the passion interval fulfilling the sign of Jonah) and merely re-specifies the location/scope; the Ezekiel texts do genuinely establish Jerusalem as 'the midst of the land,' giving the reading a scriptural hook. However, Ezekiel never uses the phrase 'heart of the earth,' and swapping the tomb/realm-of-the-dead referent for a city is replacement of the central identification, not a boundary adjustment.
